targetText:
Capitalist production is not merely the production of commodities,
it is essentially the production of surplus-value. The labourer produces,
not for himself, but for capital. It no longer suffices, therefore, that
he should simply produce. He must produce surplus-value. That labourer
alone is productive, who produces surplus-value for the capitalist, and
thus works for the self-expansion of capital.
explanation: Under capitalism, production exists not merely to create useful goods, but fundamentally to generate surplus value. A worker is "productive" only insofar as they produce profit for their employer.
summary: Productive labour under capitalism: a worker is productive only if they produce surplus-value for capital.
context: Part V, Chapter 16: Absolute and Relative Surplus-Value

targetText:
The product ceases to be the direct product of the
individual, and becomes a social product, produced in common by a collective
labourer, i.e., by a combination of workmen, each of whom takes
only a part, greater or less, in the manipulation of the subject of their
labour.
explanation: Under capitalist cooperation, the product is no longer made by a single person from start to finish. It becomes a collective social product, yet its entire value is appropriated by the capitalist.
summary: The collective labourer and separation of head and hand: production becomes socialized while hand and brain are alienated from each other.
context: Part V, Chapter 16: Absolute and Relative Surplus-Value
